newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani committee recommends cotton buffer stock.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani committee recommends cotton buffer stock.

text.p: A textile committee set up by Pakistan Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif proposed on Thursday that the government finance a four-month buffer stock of cotton.

In a report obtained by Reuters, the committee made 55 recommendations aimed at ensuring that the textile industry has access to raw material at stable prices, has adequate financing, uses all its capacity and concentrates on value-added exports.

It said a government-financed consortium should be set up in the private sector to hold a buffer stock of four months' supply of cotton. This could be sold on a no-profit, no-loss basis at times of crisis to keep textile mills running.

The committee, which grouped businessmen and government officials, said the consortium should have a board of governors on which growers, ginners, the Karachi Cotton Association and the All Pakistan Textile Mills Association were represented.
It proposed setting up a Textile Council headed by the industries and investment minister to formulate textile policy, oversee implementation and get tax and duty anomalies removed.

The report said the government should maintain the present policy of free trade in cotton, but should not allow physical shipment of cotton until December each year when final estimates of the cotton crop are available.
It said export of polyester fibre "over and above domestic requirement" should be allowed.

Import taxes on dyes, chemicals and auxiliaries should be reduced to a minimum, while duties on value-added machinery and spare parts should also be cut. Certain local taxes should be rationalised and should not be levied on exporters.
The report said textile units that have closed but are commercially viable should be given financial relief.
To meet a need for increased credit lines, the enforcement of prudential regulations, relating to debt equity ratio and current ratio, should be relaxed for three years, it said.
Duty rebates for exporters should be rationalised and disbursed more efficiently. Utility rates should be reduced or frozen and surcharges withdrawn, the report said.
"An export strategy should be developed by gradually shifting all the incentives to production and export of value-added products," the report said.
The report was due to be submitted to the government on Thursday or Friday, one of its authors said.
